subtitle: Optional background on regional culture frameworks: where they come from, what they measured, and why clusters say nothing about any person or about Minnesota communities.
audience: Optional, for DHS and DSD employees who have met a regional chart or cultural profile at work, or who are curious where those charts come from. No other course depends on it.

lessons.title: What regional frameworks are, and what they say nothing about
objectives: Describe how the GLOBE research program grouped societies into ten cultural clusters.
Name the ten GLOBE societal clusters.
Explain what the cluster data measured and what it did not measure.
Explain why clusters say nothing about any person or about Minnesota communities.
lessons.teaching:
You may come across charts that sort the world into regions and describe how people in each supposedly communicate or lead. One influential framework comes from GLOBE, the Global Leadership and Organizational Behavior Effectiveness research program. The study reported in 2004 drew on more than seventeen thousand middle managers in sixty-two societies. It examined perceived practices and values in organizations and societies. Researchers used prior literature to propose clusters and tested those groupings against survey data. The 2002 paper by Vipin Gupta, Paul Hanges and Peter Dorfman used data from sixty-one nations to test proposed groupings. Its abstract reports support for ten clusters: Anglo, Germanic Europe, Nordic Europe, Latin Europe, Eastern Europe, Latin America, Sub-Saharan Africa, Arab (named Middle East in some later GLOBE writing), South Asia and Confucian Asia.

Cluster studies can provide historical context for questions about organizations and societies. They cannot predict the preferences, behavior or needs of any individual. One separate overview of cultural clusters is David Livermore’s Expand Your Borders (2013). The groupings in this course are described by the GLOBE research program.

It is just as important to know what the data did not measure. The respondents were managers in organizations, not a cross-section of each society. The results are averages for societies, usually countries, not descriptions of individuals. They were collected at a particular time, and societies change. Many people and peoples do not fit national boundaries: the Hmong live across several countries, Dakota and Anishinaabe nations are sovereign nations within what is now Minnesota, and many Minnesotans have heritage in more than one society or grew up here with parents from elsewhere. A national average cannot show the full range of religious, linguistic, regional and class differences within a country. Introductory textbooks that teach GLOBE make the same point, warning that relying solely on such frameworks can be misleading.

So hold two ideas together. Cluster research asks empirical questions, but its claims depend on sampling, measurement, analysis and context. A large sample alone does not establish that it represents everyone. And a cluster describes a statistical tendency across a group of societies. Clusters say nothing about any person, and they say nothing about Minnesota communities. They were not built from Minnesota residents, and they cannot tell you how the person on the other side of the table communicates, decides or builds trust. To learn about a community here, go to the program’s community briefs and to the people themselves. The rest of this course is about using the map without mistaking it for the territory.
lessons.keyPoint: GLOBE’s ten clusters group societies by similarities in managers’ survey responses. They say nothing about any person or about Minnesota communities.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Before a video call with a provider association whose leaders include several people who emigrated from Latin America, Grace, a DSD contract manager, skims a summary of the Latin America cluster. It notes a tendency, on average, to place value on relationships and group loyalty. Grace plans to open the call with ten minutes of personal conversation and to avoid discussing the contract details until the end. Her colleague Luis, who grew up in Minneapolis, says the association's leaders are known for being very businesslike.
lessons.question: What is the best way for Grace to use what she read?
choices: Keep her plan, since the cluster research is based on thousands of respondents.
Ignore the cluster summary entirely, since Luis has more direct knowledge.

Treat the summary as no evidence about these leaders and only as a reminder to prepare for more than one style: set a clear agenda with room for relationship building, and ask them at the start how they would like to use the time.
feedback: A large sample does not by itself establish representative or reliable conclusions for an entire society. This summary also does not establish these leaders’ preferences. Prepare usable options and ask the people involved.

Luis may have useful experience with these leaders. Treat it as context to check, not a rule for each person. Grace should neither assign a cluster style nor replace it with another fixed expectation.

This is the strongest response. The summary is not evidence about these leaders. Grace uses it only as a reminder to prepare for more than one style and to ask them, so the people involved shape the meeting.
lessons.reflection: When you read about a cultural pattern tied to a region, what is your first instinct: to apply it, to reject it, or to test it? What shapes that instinct?
lessons.action: Choose a regional chart you have encountered. Identify its study date, respondents and level of analysis. Write two reasons it cannot establish an individual’s preferences, without labeling a real colleague.

check.question: What did the GLOBE cluster research primarily measure?
check.correct: Average responses from managers in organizations about practices and values in their societies, grouped into clusters of similar societies.
wrong: The personality traits of every person living in each country.
Which cultures are more effective or advanced than others.
check.feedback: GLOBE compared societies using managers' survey responses. It produced averages for societies, not profiles of individuals, and grouping societies by similarity is not the same as ranking them.

lessons.title: Cultural intelligence: questions for context, power and access
objectives: Describe cultural intelligence as a broad practice of learning and working across differences.
Identify how reflection, context, communication and access can inform a situation.
Explain the limits of regional research and consider organizational power and barriers.
Identify a person-centered way to improve participation in DHS or DSD work.
lessons.teaching:
This program uses cultural intelligence to mean learning and working across differences. It draws on several fields, including sociology, anthropology, psychology, education and communication. Disability justice, person-centered practice, intercultural development and psychological safety offer further perspectives. No single model defines the whole program. Ang and colleagues studied a specific model with four dimensions, often called CQ. That research does not establish that every approach used here is the same or has the same evidence.

Regional research offers limited context. Group averages cannot establish what a person thinks, needs or prefers. Ask what matters to the person, consider their choices and access needs, and check your assumptions against evidence.

Look at power within the organization too. Who sets the rules? Whose knowledge counts? Who can take part, and what barriers do policies create? Curiosity and flexible communication can help, but good intentions alone do not resolve unequal access.

Reflection can support learning. This course does not assign a score, predict someone’s performance or replace agency duties. More comments after a meeting may show that another way to contribute was useful. That change alone does not establish psychological safety or explain why someone was quiet before. Ask for feedback and review what the new option actually changed.
lessons.keyPoint: Use regional research as limited context, not a personal script. Ask people directly and examine access, power and organizational practices.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Jin, a new DSD supervisor, has read several regional culture summaries and can describe patterns for most of the ten clusters. In team meetings, though, she runs the agenda the same way every time and is surprised when some staff rarely speak. Her manager, Paula, suggests she look at how she is using what she knows. Paula points out that two quieter staff members wrote thoughtful comments on a draft afterward, so they clearly have views to share.
lessons.question: What would help Jin make the meeting more accessible and inclusive?
choices: Ask staff about useful ways to contribute, offer more than one accessible option and check whether participation changes.
Read more regional summaries and assume they explain each staff member’s preferences.
Tell staff to be more enthusiastic about the existing meeting format.
feedback: This response checks the meeting design with staff and creates options without assuming why any person is quiet.
More reading cannot establish an individual’s preferences or remove a barrier in the meeting format.
Enthusiasm alone does not address whether the meeting offers accessible ways to contribute.
lessons.reflection: Where might a routine meeting or decision give some people more influence than others? What could you ask or change to improve access?
lessons.action: Before your next meeting that includes people with different working styles, write down one assumption you hold about how the meeting should run and one way you will check it during the meeting.

check.question: How should regional research such as GLOBE be used in this program?
check.correct: As limited group-level context, alongside individual perspectives and attention to organizational power and access.
wrong: As the whole definition of cultural intelligence.
As a reliable guide to exactly how every individual will behave.
check.feedback: Group-level research cannot predict a person’s preferences. Use it cautiously, ask individuals, and examine policies, participation and power.

lessons.title: The ecological fallacy: group averages do not predict individuals
objectives: Define the ecological fallacy in plain language.
Explain why a society-level average cannot tell you where any individual falls.
Identify examples of the ecological fallacy in everyday workplace and service decisions.
Compare a stereotype with a pattern used only to write a question.
lessons.teaching:
The ecological fallacy is the error of assuming that relationships observed for groups necessarily hold for individuals. The statistician David Freedman explained it with a classic example: finding higher suicide rates in societies with more Protestants does not show that Protestants themselves were more likely to die by suicide. Group data and individual data answer different questions. A pattern across groups can even reverse when you look at individuals.

Cluster frameworks are group data. If the average response from one cluster's managers leaned toward respect for hierarchy, that tells you something about the societies in that cluster compared with others. It does not tell you whether a particular colleague who grew up in one of those societies prefers a hierarchical style. The spread of individuals within a society is usually wide, and the averages of two societies can differ while many individuals from each overlap. Migration, generation, profession, faith, disability, personal history and organizational setting may also matter. These factors warrant attention; they do not provide another formula for predicting the person.

In practice, the ecological fallacy shows up in small moments. A hiring panelist reads a candidate's hesitation to self-promote as a cultural trait rather than asking a follow-up question. A supervisor assumes a new employee from a certain region will not want to disagree in meetings and stops inviting their view. A case manager assumes a family from a particular country will not want outside help. Each substitutes a group-based explanation for evidence about the person. A stereotype can arise from a misapplied average, an unsupported claim or a false belief. Calling an idea research-based does not make it appropriate for an individual decision.

A group pattern may suggest a question or a change to a system, but it never predicts the person in front of you. Offer accessible options, ask the person and respect their choices. Decisions with real consequences must follow the relevant facts and responsible process.
lessons.keyPoint: A cluster average describes a group of societies, not the person in front of you. Turn a pattern into a question, not an expectation, and let people tell you; never base consequential decisions on group averages.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: On a hiring panel for a DSD policy role, Mark notes that one candidate, Wei, gave short answers about her own accomplishments and often said "we" instead of "I." Mark says this is typical of the Confucian Asia cluster and suggests the panel mentally adjust her scores upward. Another panelist, Ingrid, is uneasy but is not sure why. The panel's scoring guide asks every candidate to describe a policy project they led and their specific role in it.
lessons.question: What should Ingrid say?
choices: Agree with Mark, since adjusting for cultural style is a fair thing to do.

Use the job-related scoring criteria and ask Human Resources about consistent, permitted follow-up prompts and any required accommodations. Clarify each candidate’s contribution without guessing a cultural explanation or adjusting scores by group.
Say that culture has nothing to do with interview behavior, so the panel should score the answers as given with no follow-up.
feedback: Mark's intent is generous, but guessing Wei's style from a cluster average and adjusting her score is the ecological fallacy and is not a consistent, job-related process.

This is the strongest response. It keeps scoring grounded in job-related evidence and follows the hiring process. Consistency does not mean denying an accommodation; confirm permitted prompts and access arrangements with Human Resources.

The panel should follow the established interview process and seek HR guidance if a barrier or unclear answer needs attention. Neither a cultural guess nor an unapproved change to the interview is a sound solution.
lessons.reflection: Can you recall a time someone assumed something about you based on a group you belong to, even a flattering assumption? What would you have preferred they do?
lessons.action: Using Wei’s fictional case, identify the assumption and draft a job-related follow-up to discuss with Human Resources. Do not alter a live interview process or scoring without the required authorization.

check.question: Which statement is an example of the ecological fallacy?
check.correct: Because one cluster's average leaned toward indirect communication, this colleague from that region must prefer indirect feedback.
wrong: Averages for two clusters differed on how they rated hierarchy.
Individuals within the same society vary widely in communication style.
check.feedback: Comparing group averages is a legitimate use of group data, and recognizing individual variation is accurate. The fallacy is moving from a group average to a conclusion about a particular person.

lessons.title: Turning a cluster pattern into questions in everyday work
objectives: Plan how to turn a cluster pattern into a question.
Distinguish preparing for more than one style from predicting a single style.
Explain how to drop a pattern based on what a person or partner tells you.
Draft a short preparation note for a meeting using this question-first approach.
lessons.teaching:
If you do use a cluster pattern, and you never have to, how should you use it? The answer is to turn it into a question you ask, never an expectation of the person. In this program, that is one way to practice preparation, awareness and checking. It uses knowledge to widen what you prepare for, rather than narrow what you expect.

A simple sequence works well. First, name the pattern: "Research suggests societies in this cluster tended, on average, to place more emphasis on relationships before business." Second, turn it on yourself: what is my own default here, and what would I miss if the meeting ran only that way? Getting straight to an agenda may reflect a habit, job demand or organizational norm. Consider whether it fits this meeting rather than assigning it a cultural cause. Third, list the options you can offer: a clear agenda, time for introductions for those who want it, and more than one way to contribute. Fourth, ask, and let the person choose: "How would you like to use our time today?" Fifth, revise: what the person tells you replaces the pattern. Then, importantly, do not carry that person's preference onto the next person from the same region.

One further habit keeps those questions honest: look beyond national culture. DHS, professions, disability communities and generations can each contain varied practices and experiences. None is a single style shared by every member. A county social worker and a state policy analyst from the same background may still work very differently.

Consider how assumptions about communication, time, decision-making and authority shape your own habits, your team and its processes. These questions are not labels for people or communities.

In DHS and DSD work, this approach has a narrow use: noticing your own defaults and widening what you prepare for. It tells you nothing about a Minnesota community or the person you are meeting. To learn about them, go to the program's community briefs, community partners and the people served. It never justifies a group-based judgment in a formal decision. Required accommodations and lawful, individualized decisions still follow their proper processes. A framework can remind you to prepare for more than one style. The people you work with give you the answers.
lessons.keyPoint: Use a cluster pattern only to name your own default and widen the options you prepare. Then ask, let the person choose, and revise. Never carry one person's answer onto the next person.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Fatima, a DSD program specialist, is preparing for her first meeting with a new Tribal liaison, Joseph, and a county supervisor, Linda, to plan a joint training. Fatima wants to use what she has read in some regional culture summaries. She has also read that tribal governments have their own protocols. She is unsure how to prepare without making assumptions about either person.
lessons.question: What preparation approach is best?
choices: Prepare a clear draft agenda with space for introductions, ask both at the start how they would like to proceed, and check with DHS Tribal relations staff about any protocol that applies to working with the Tribal government.
Use the Anglo cluster profile for Linda and skip preparation for Joseph, since Tribal nations are not in the cluster data.
Avoid preparing at all, so she does not bring any assumptions into the room.
feedback: This is the strongest response. It asks the participants about the meeting while checking government-to-government responsibilities with the appropriate staff. An informal planning meeting or a liaison’s participation does not by itself satisfy formal consultation duties under section 10.65.

Assigning Linda a cluster profile from a guess about her background is the ecological fallacy, and noticing that the cluster data does not cover Tribal nations should lead to asking, not to less preparation.
Skipping preparation does not remove assumptions; it just leaves your own defaults unexamined.
lessons.reflection: Think about an upcoming interaction with someone whose working style you do not yet know. What is your own default style, and how might it shape the meeting if you do not name it?
lessons.action: Write a short preparation note for one upcoming meeting: your own default, one or two other styles to prepare for, the question you will ask to find out, and how you will adjust.

check.question: What is the main difference between using a cluster pattern as a source of questions and using it as a stereotype?
check.correct: A question leaves the answer to the person and is asked fresh of each person; a stereotype is applied as a fixed expectation.
wrong: A question is based on research, while a stereotype is always invented.
Questions are only used by researchers, not in daily work.
check.feedback: The distinction is how the idea is used, not whether it carries a research label. A respectful question leaves room for an individual answer and revision. A stereotype imposes an expectation, whether its starting point was a finding, a rumor or a false claim.

cards.back: Ten groups of societies with similar average survey responses about cultural practices and values: Anglo, Germanic Europe, Nordic Europe, Latin Europe, Eastern Europe, Latin America, Sub-Saharan Africa, Arab or Middle East, South Asia and Confucian Asia. They say nothing about any person or about Minnesota communities.
A broad practice of learning and working across differences, informed by multiple disciplines and attention to access, power and lived experience.
The error of assuming that relationships observed for groups necessarily hold for individuals.
A pattern used only to widen what you prepare for and to write a question you would ask anyone. It never sets an expectation of the person.
Using knowledge to plan for an interaction, notice when something is not working, and check assumptions as you go.

aid.heading: Before you use a cluster profile
items: Remember it describes averages for societies, based mostly on managers' responses.
Name your own default style first.
List reasons a specific person might not fit, such as migration, generation, faith, profession or disability.
Do not treat sampled national categories as profiles of Tribal nations or peoples who live across borders.

aid.heading: Turn a pattern into a question
items: State the pattern as a tendency of societies, not a fact about a person.
List the options you can offer.
Ask, using questions you would ask anyone, and let the person choose.
Revise, and do not carry one person's answer onto the next.

aid.heading: Guardrails
items: Never use a cluster to describe a Minnesota community or any person.
Never use a cluster profile in hiring, discipline, eligibility or service decisions.
Do not rate or label colleagues' cultural intelligence.
Use current community briefs as background, check their sources and dates, and hear from varied partners and the people affected.
Consult Tribal relations staff about government-to-government protocols and any formal consultation required; ordinary engagement is not a substitute.

sources.title: Livermore, D. (2013). Expand your borders: Discover ten cultural clusters. Cultural Intelligence Center.
sources.note: Publisher sample reviewed as historical background. Its group profiles and advice are not reproduced or adopted as individual predictions.

sources.title: Journal of World Business — Gupta, Hanges and Dorfman, Cultural clusters: methodology and findings (2002)
sources.note: Publisher abstract supports ten proposed clusters tested with 61-nation data. Full article was not accessible; no full-method appraisal is claimed.

sources.title: OpenStax (Rice University) — Principles of Management, The GLOBE Framework
sources.note: Introductory summary of GLOBE's scope, about seventeen thousand managers in sixty-two societies, and its caution that relying solely on such frameworks can be misleading.

sources.title: Cultural Intelligence Center — Frequently Asked Questions about cultural intelligence
sources.note: The Center’s account of its specific CQ model and terminology, not the definition of this broader program or an independent validation of every effectiveness claim.

sources.title: Management and Organization Review — Ang, Van Dyne, Koh and colleagues, Cultural Intelligence: Its Measurement and Effects on Cultural Judgment and Decision Making, Cultural Adaptation and Task Performance (2007, author manuscript)
sources.note: Author manuscript abstract, introduction and limitations reviewed: four dimensions, a twenty-item scale and context-specific associations. It does not validate this course or every approach in the program.

sources.title: University of California, Berkeley, Department of Statistics — David A. Freedman, The Ecological Fallacy
sources.note: Definition of the ecological fallacy as assuming group relationships hold for individuals, with classic examples. Supports the course's central caution.

sources.title: GLOBE — 2004 and 2007 studies
sources.note: Primary research-program account of sample, measures and literature-informed cluster testing; distinct from the 2002 article’s 61-nation scope.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes 10.65 — Government-to-government relationship
sources.note: Formal Tribal consultation, responsible governmental participants and duties; not interchangeable with a routine meeting.
